notes.text: For more than 8, bake the croutons on two sheet pans and swap their shelves halfway, and cook the chicken in two batches.

move.title: Whisk it, cube it, toss it
move.body: A dressing is a sauce for a salad, and whisking is how you make it smooth. Today you'll whisk a creamy Caesar dressing, cut bread into even cubes and bake them into crunchy croutons, cook chicken, and toss it all with crisp romaine.

callback.body: In your dicing lesson you cut planks, then sticks, then cubes. Croutons are the same move with bread, just bigger cubes, about the size of a game die.

why.title: Even cubes, even crunch
why.body: Little cubes dry out and brown before big ones. If the bread cubes are all about the same size, every crouton turns golden and crunchy at the same moment, with none burnt and none still soft in the middle.

why.title: The oven dries, the oil browns
why.body: Bread is soft because it holds water. In the oven the water dries out, and the bread turns crisp all the way through. The oil on the outside helps it brown and gives it flavor.

why.title: Why the dressing stays creamy
why.body: Oil and lemon juice don't mix on their own. Mayonnaise holds them together: it's oil already beaten into egg yolk in tiny drops. Whisk the rest of the oil in slowly, a little at a time, and the dressing stays thick and smooth instead of separating.

why.title: No raw eggs here
why.body: Old-style Caesar dressing uses raw egg yolks, which can carry germs that make people sick. Store mayonnaise is made with pasteurized eggs, which have been gently heated to kill germs. So this dressing has the creamy egg taste and is safe to eat without cooking.

why.title: Dry leaves hold the dressing
why.body: Dressing slides right off wet lettuce, and the water left on the leaves makes it thin and bland. Lettuce patted dry in a towel lets the dressing cling to every leaf.

wrong.sign: The dressing is too thick to pour
wrong.fix: Whisk in a teaspoon of water at a time until it runs slowly off the whisk.

wrong.sign: The dressing looks oily and separated
wrong.fix: The oil went in too fast. Put a spoonful of mayonnaise in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the separated dressing into it.

wrong.sign: The croutons are still soft in the middle
wrong.fix: Bake them a few minutes more. They crisp up more as they cool, too.
It sat too long after tossing, or the lettuce was wet. Toss only right before eating, and keep croutons on top.

quiz.q: Why does this dressing use store mayonnaise instead of raw egg yolks?
choices: It's made with pasteurized eggs, so it's safe
quiz.explain: Pasteurized eggs have been gently heated to kill germs, so the dressing is safe without cooking.

quiz.q: How do you add the olive oil to the dressing?
quiz.explain: A little at a time keeps the dressing thick and smooth.

substitutions.note: Use about 6 slices of gluten-free bread for each baguette. It browns faster, so check it a few minutes early.
Greek yogurt makes a tangier dressing. Taste it before adding all the lemon juice.

steps.text: Turn the oven on to 375°F.
Cut the baguette into slices about ¾ inch thick.
steps.tip: Use a gentle back-and-forth sawing motion. Pressing straight down squashes soft bread.

steps.text: Lay a few slices flat. Cut them into strips as wide as the slices are thick, then cut across the strips to make cubes.
steps.look: Cubes about the size of a game die, all close to the same size.

steps.text: Put the cubes in the large bowl. Add {qty:olive-oil} olive oil, the garlic powder, and {qty:salt} salt, and toss with your hands until every cube is coated. Spread them on the sheet pan in one layer.
With oven mitts on, put the pan in the oven.
Pull the pan out with oven mitts, stir the croutons with the spatula, and bake until golden.
steps.look: Golden brown, and they feel dry and light when you tap one.

steps.text: Take the pan out, turn off the oven, and leave the croutons on the pan to cool. Wipe out the bowl for the salad.
Lay the chicken on the plate. Sprinkle both sides with the chicken's salt and the pepper.
Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw chicken or its package touched.
Heat the vegetable oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Use the tongs to lay the chicken in the pan, smooth side down, laying each piece down away from you. Put the tongs in the sink, and don't use them again for cooked food.
Wash your hands, and put the raw-chicken plate in the sink. From here on, use the clean spatula.
Leave the chicken alone while the bottom browns.
steps.look: Golden brown underneath, and it lets go of the pan when you nudge it.

steps.text: Flip each piece with the spatula. Turn the heat down to medium and put the lid on.
steps.tip: The lid traps heat, so thick pieces cook through to the middle before the outside gets too dark.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the thickest piece. It needs to read at least 165°F. If it doesn't, put the lid back on, cook 2 more minutes, and check again.
Turn off the stove. Move the chicken to the clean cutting board with the spatula and let it rest.
Peel the garlic and mince it into tiny bits. Put it in the small bowl.
Add the mayonnaise, lemon juice, mustard, the Worcestershire sauce if you're using it, and the parmesan for the dressing. Whisk until smooth.
Keep whisking while you pour in the dressing's olive oil a little at a time. Whisk in water, 1 teaspoon at a time, until the dressing runs slowly off the whisk.
steps.look: Smooth, creamy, and pale, about as thick as melted ice cream.

steps.text: Pull the romaine leaves apart, rinse them in the colander, and pat them dry in the kitchen towel. Stack a few leaves, cut them across into strips about an inch wide, and put them in the large bowl.
Slice the rested chicken into thin strips.
Right before eating, pour the dressing over the lettuce and toss until every leaf is coated. Top with the chicken, the croutons, and the rest of the parmesan.
steps.tip: Keep the croutons on top so they stay crunchy.

substitutions.note: Use about 6 slices of gluten-free bread for each baguette. It browns faster, so check it a few minutes early.

add.title: Yolks to 160°F
add.body: Pasteurized eggs are heat-treated in the shell, and the USDA says they can be used raw. This app goes one step further and cooks every egg to 160°F. Yolks whisked with lemon juice over gentle steam thicken at that temperature, and they still make a mayonnaise-style emulsion once cooled.

creamy.title: Building an emulsion
creamy.body: Egg yolk is the emulsifier: its lecithin coats each droplet of oil so the droplets can't join. The first oil goes in a drop at a time, because a few large droplets have nothing to cling to; once the emulsion forms, a thin stream is fine. A mix of neutral oil and olive oil keeps the dressing from turning bitter.

safe-eggs.title: From scratch, still safe
safe-eggs.body: The classic dressing is raw egg yolk and anchovy. Here the yolks are pasteurized and cooked to 160°F, so the dressing tastes like the original without the risk. Store mayonnaise is made with pasteurized eggs too.

add.text: Heat the oven to 375°F. Cut the baguette into 2-cm cubes and toss them with {qty:olive-oil} olive oil, the garlic powder, and {qty:salt} salt. Spread them on the sheet pan.
Bake the croutons, stirring halfway, until golden and dry through. Cool them on the pan.
add.look: Golden, and light when you tap one.

add.text: Season the chicken on both sides with the chicken's salt and the pepper.
Wash your hands and wipe down anything the raw chicken touched.
Heat the vegetable oil in the skillet over medium-high until it shimmers. Lay the chicken in smooth side down and sear without moving it.
Wash your hands and move the raw-chicken plate and tongs to the sink.
Flip the chicken, turn the heat to medium, and cover.
Probe the thickest piece: 165°F. If it's short, cover and check again in 2 minutes.
Rest the chicken on a clean board while you make the dressing.
Separate the eggs, dropping the yolks into the heatproof bowl. Keep the whites for another use.
Wash your hands and wipe the counter.
Whisk the lemon juice and 1 tablespoon of water into the yolks. Set the bowl over barely simmering water and whisk constantly until thick enough to hold a trail.
Probe the yolks: 160°F. Take the bowl off the water and keep whisking for 1 minute to cool it.
Mince the garlic with the anchovies, if using, and a pinch of salt, then press it into a paste with the flat of the knife. Whisk it into the yolks with the mustard and Worcestershire.
Whisk in the dressing's oils drop by drop for the first quarter, then in a thin stream, until thick and glossy.
add.look: Thick enough to hold a ribbon on the surface for a second.

add.text: Whisk in the dressing's parmesan, then water a teaspoon at a time until it pours slowly. Taste and adjust with lemon and salt.
Wash and dry the romaine, and cut it across into 2.5-cm ribbons.
Slice the chicken across the grain, ⅜ inch thick.
Toss the romaine with two thirds of the dressing just before serving. Top with the chicken, croutons, and remaining parmesan, and pass the rest of the dressing.
add.tip: Refrigerate leftover dressing and use it within 4 days.
